utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to your new courtroom. But we are likely to be here for just a fortnight. So we'll return to our familiar old place. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution appearing with Mr. George Huber, who is just out of the courtroom for a few seconds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I am Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: God morning, my name is Niko Duric, attorney from Zagreb, Croatia representing Mr. Mucic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: My name is Niko Duric, attorney at law from Zagreb, Croatian and I represent Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Fortunately, my colleagues, Mr. Olujic and Mr. Kuzmanovic are out of town, and they should be back at the end of this week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence Counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic along with my colleague, Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and along with my colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Mr. Esad Landzo. Ms. Boler is temporarily absent. She will be present in just a moment. I would also like to say that we have only one set of earphones here. So I think that would be a problem coming up during the session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I just can't see him, but I am just wondering if Mr. Delalic is here, and if not, maybe the record should reflect something about that in the reasons, just for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the last time, after the appearances, I was going to get up and say that my client is still not feeling very well. He has an additional examination today. I believe that you may have received an official notice of that from the detention unit. I have talked to Mr. Delalic this morning, and he gave me instructions that we can continue without his presence. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In things of this nature, don't you think, as counsel, you needed a medical certificate to satisfy that he is unable to come, and that he might come when he is fit. Because we have taken -- it should not continue for too long.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I -- my understanding is, that he is feeling better. We believe that after today's examination he will rejoin the trial. He was examined on Thursday. We have his finding. We also have faxed our request for an urgent examination, based on the pains that Mr. Delalic has suffered. Based on this fax, he has been re-examined yesterday and today. We will submit the findings that are made today. But we believe that he will be able to rejoin us tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well I think we expect him to rejoin tomorrow morning. Mr. Karabdic, I think we'll start with your witness today, this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Our first witness will be Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I suddenly found a courtroom that is smarter than I am with all the electronic equipment. It may take me a minute to figure out what I am doing. Your honours, just for the Court's planning, this witness, from our standpoint, will be very brief, short, and the next witness should not be excessively long either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness take the oath, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask something of the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been subpoenaed here and as a person who feels offended by this, I would like to know who asked this and what were the reasons, and why am I asked to testify against my own will here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he takes the oath, I think the Trial Chamber might want to explain it, or I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly take the oath. When you sit down, we will explain to you what is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, you have just indicated that you are unwilling to come to testify; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: No, that is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are willing to come, even if no subpoenas were issued for you to come, you could have come despite a subpoena not being issued?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I must say, just so that you understand a little bit why I am not clear about this situation. I am a physician, a surgeon, a general surgeon. Throughout the war I did my job honestly and in good faith. When the International Criminal Tribunal was established, I was very glad. I have personal reasons for that, because my mother and sister are victims of the genocide. This is why I salute and I support any action which would lead to punishment and sentences of everybody -- anybody who has committed any war crimes. I am a professional. I know what my job is and I know what the rules are in my profession. And let me tell you something, when Ms. Edina Residovic asked me to testify for Mr. Delalic, I accepted that, and the attorney here can testify to that. The statement which I gave at that time, I am ready to confirm in any form anywhere in the world. I have given no other statement. I have -- I'm met by hundreds of people and I don't talk to them. There are written requests. If I receive a written request, can I meet with people and we can discuss about what I could talk about. However, I never received any such request. This attorney that I am referring to, met me casually in the hallway and I did not want to talk to him. I said, "Please put it down in writing and send it to me." This was all informal. I had expected him to -- him to write down what he wanted to do. However, he showed up again, unannounced, and then I told him that I wouldn't want to come here. I did not refuse to come. I wanted to come as an expert witness. I am not a fact witness here. I cannot testify to certain things. I'm a physician. So this is why -- this is where the answer to the question is about my coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we now understand. That was not the impression of your -- of counsel. Could counsel think you were unwilling and, therefore, they have to issue this subpoena to enable you to come? If there are any obstacles in your way, because if there are any obstacles in your way, then a subpoena would help you to overcome them.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I understand you completely, but please, do understand me as well. I have come here to speak the truth. I will say the truth. I cannot speak about what they do not say, because asking a person to say something that he doesn't know is senseless. I have also given a hypocritical oath and I have helped anyone, regardless of race, colour of skin, for me they were all just sick people or wounded people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can now deal with counsel and answer counsel's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, will you state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I am Dr. Sead Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, doctor, how are you employed at the present time?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I work in the general hospital in Konjic as general surgeon, and I am also director of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about your training and experience. Just a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me just, if this witness is not being called as an expert witness and Mr. Moran has represented several times that he is not, I would just believe his training and experience is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would think that the Trial Chamber might want to know who they are listening to, but whatever makes the Court happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's part of his address, and everything about him. He could indicate his training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, tell the Trial Chamber about your training and experience.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: As I stated, my name is Sead Buturovic. I am a general surgeon. I graduated from a medical school in Belgrade in 1977. I was third in my class, and then I became a general practitioner in my hometown of Konjic. After that a couple of years later, I went to Travnik to specialise, because there was only in health centre. In '80 I completed the -- specialisation in Sarajevo and then since then I have become the general surgeon. Since, in Konjic there was only health centre, there was no surgery theatre there, and I was ambitious. This is why I went to specialisation. I would go to Sarajevo to the military school, which is now General Hospital, which was a military hospital. And I went there once a week until the war came. When the war started, I was a general surgeon at the health centre in Konjic, and the situation was such as it was. Myself and several of my colleagues organised war surgery as the beginnings of the future war, the hospital, in order to treat the wounded and injured, which had started arriving there, the conditions were very difficult. We had no conditions. We had no instruments, we had no supplies. We had no personnel which would be able to help us, to assist us in this. I was the only surgeon there in the health centre with people who had never seen a war wound before, with people who had never entered the surgery. People who did not know what a wounded person was, what an injured person was, because until the war we would send all serious cases to Mostar or Sarajevo. In those days we could not send any patients there, given what had happened in the beginning of the war, the communication lines had been cut off, and the wounded and the injured kept arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Listen just a second. This will go a lot quicker if you will just listen to my questions and answer them. I think we've talked about that. Doctor, do you remember meeting with our investigator, Mr. Karabdic's investigator Nehir Serdarevic?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Investigator? Which investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The investigator that we hired, a dark headed gentleman downstairs in the witness room with you this morning. Do you remember meeting with Nehir?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Oh, yes. This meeting took place about ten days ago. Not earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Nehir that you did not want to appear here voluntarily because your wife had had a financial dispute with John Ackerman, who had retained her as an investigator? Do you remember telling him that?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: That's really ridiculous. As I said, I am a professional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Questioning the credibility of your own witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your honour, I am asking the Trial Chamber to let me treat him as a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then why examine him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, he is the person that can testify about some specific facts involving my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A hostile witness is one who is not prepared to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or who is not -- where I am from, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he gives any answers which you find are not -- do not support your case, then your case is that really he's not speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moran, we've not really seen when you declare him a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the practice that I am used to, all that allows me to do is ask leading questions on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You go ahead and ask until you find that his evidence is quite contrary to what you've called him for, then you can do that. But there is no basis for treating him as a hostile witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, sometime in September, 1996, do you recall examining some records involving my client, Hazim Delic and preparation a report based on the contents of those records?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I recall that certain -- a gentleman, I believe his name was Brackovic, came to the institution where I work. I believe it could have been in '96. And he was looking for documents, that is a written report on whether Mr. Delic was treated at our institution. By looking at our records, and you have to realise that we had just gone through the war, our archives were incomplete. We were taking more care of patients, more than papers, and so we had some documents. And we found certain things, and I had signed that. We found a document saying that he was treated for a certain condition, and this was submitted to me. And this finding, and this opinion, I signed as a director of the institution where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you don't remember Mr. Delic from Adam, do you? You don't remember his case at all?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Listen, in those days I would receive 30 to 40 patients daily. I spent a lot of time in the surgery room. I slept very little. I worked practically 24 hours. For three years I slept in the hospital. I do not recall whether he came there. I could not claim that. It is possible that he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, basically, your testimony here is just simply based on your review of the records?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Exclusively on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the usher's permission, did you produce that document this morning at my request? Your Honour, this was provided to the Prosecutor about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D106/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, that's all you remember about the treatment of Mr. Delic, or that's all you know about.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Believe me, it's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I provided an English translation. I didn't? I thought I did. It's on the bottom. Take a look.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew there had to be an English version because the Serbo-Croatian wouldn't do me any good either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And all that you know about this case is that you repaired his right Achilles tendon and that he was hospitalised in your facility from 21 to 25, May, 1992. Doctor, you have to say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: It's what's stated there. Yes, that is what is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. But, let me tell you, by reviewing the documents available in our hospital, I signed the document by reviewing the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, doctor. Doctor, in this type of surgery, is it common that a person would be in a plaster cast after the surgery?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We have filed a motion which says, first of all, that there is no notification of special defence. Second of all, this witness has expressly been called as a fact witness. And to ask this witness questions about what's common and what's not common are clearly questions of opinion, based upon his expertise as a doctor, and I believe they are not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If it makes Ms. McHenry a little happier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, when you performed surgery, as outlined in this report, do you put a plaster cast on a patient's leg?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I can say the following. It is usual that following such injuries a patient is put in a plaster cast, and it is possible that I did put one on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that I am Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. We have met twice before this trial.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And this is what I had just pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, is it true that on the basis of the records available in your hospital, you provided to the Defence of Mr. Delalic a document regarding the number of victims starting in May, 1992, for the duration of the war of all people who died in this hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, is it correct, that based on the knowledge of you as a physician who worked honestly throughout this war, that the number which you have in your records at the hospital about the injured and dead is much lower than the actual number of the injured and the dead in all of the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I cannot say that. Certainly, we have provided the records of the hospital, which does not dovetail with the records of what happened in the territory of the town. We have just provided the records that were available at the hospital. So whether the number is larger or lower, we do not -- I cannot speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, during your examination in chief you said that as early as May you needed to turn a small health centre into a surgical hospital, so-to-speak. Is it true that for a while, maybe up until the mid-1993, you also received the wounded from the wider area, including Tarcin, Mount Igman, Pazaric, and other areas all the way up to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct and we are proud of it. We were the first organised hospital in the area between Sarajevo and Mostar. You can only imagine what this meant. This in an area which was extremely threatened by the war. And let me finish. We took care of everyone between Hrasnica, Koloscolinja (Phon), Tarcin, Pazaric, Konjic, Jablanica, all the way down to Mostar. As I said, until September, 1992, we were the only war hospital in the entire area. And I am just going to give you one piece of information. During the shelling of Hrasnica, and this is just to confirm what I am going to say, the wounded from Hrasnica were taken to the Kosovo Hospital from Sarajevo from UNPROFOR and they were captured and then whatever followed happened. So people from Hrasnica were no longer able to go to Sarajevo to the Kosovo Hospital, but, rather, they used mountain roads over the Mount Bjelasnica to Konjic, and we treated these wounded. It was not only the wounded but also the sick people that we treated from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, the Trial Chamber has sufficient information on the wartime situation in and around Sarajevo. However, you just pointed out that you were not well prepared for these conditions. You did not have enough medication and supplies. Is it true that the first supply of medications and equipment at that time to your hospital was delivered by Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. I must say that with this donation, with this donated medication and equipment and supplies, we started and I personally delivered this request for all these supplies. And we used it to treat everyone, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, regardless of who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Buturovic. You do not know anything about the duties of Mr. Delalic throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: No. I was only a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: My name is Niko Duric and I am Defence Counsel of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, who is known also under the name of Pavo. I will only ask you a couple of short questions. Could you please tell me whether you know Mr. Zdravko Mucic?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I know Zdravko Mucic from childhood because we were born and brought up in the same area of town, and the town is very small, so we all know each other. We knew each other. We were never great friends, but we knew each other since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Could you please give your opinion about Mr. Zdravko Mucic as a person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions. And I want to thank Mr. Moran for getting all this hooked up for me ahead of time. Your Honours, I wanted to ask the Court -- the Court's indulgence on a few documents that I have to present to this witness. Our copying machine was broken all weekend and we've had very little access to it, so I have the documents and I have one copy in English. I would like to ask the Court's tolerance to allow me to put it on the ELMO and furnish the Court with copies at the next break. If that would be suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am Defence Counsel for Esad Landzo. And we have met before, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: No, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You don't remember a night in a restaurant in Konjic when I came up and introduced myself and asked you if I could speak to you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: If I could just explain this a little bit further. As you can see, I cannot imagine that in this area amongst these distinguished people there are people who in such a way, during a professional dinner with my professional friend, I had no other attention. I was sitting with my friends and this person came up to me, a person that I do not know, and she asked to talk to me. If you can even imagine something like that. If this, Your Honours, is a way in which somebody can now say to me, well, you know me, I spoke to you, then I have nothing further to add. I said at the very beginning, for me there is only a written communication, and nobody has inscripted in their foreheads who they are. Even though I have grown up in Bosnia, I am not accustomed to this kind of communication. And I do not want to communicate with anybody in this way. And I do not want anybody to tell me, well, you know me. We have spoken. And this was just such an unprofessional talk. I do not know this attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, I apologise for my informal approach to you, but at that meeting when I asked if I could set up an appointment to meet with you, your response was, "You have to see my wife," wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: My wife is an attorney, and the way she represents other people, she can also represent her husband. Why not? I am not familiar with the Rules of Procedure of this Court, as my wife does, because she is an attorney and I am a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The answer could just be yes or no. Was that your response to me, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Considering the fact that this was an informal approach, for me it was inappropriate for an institution for which you work, I might have said that also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Anyway, I would like to talk about why you are here today. You are the doctor who performed surgery on the hand of Esad Landzo in 1991, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I must say, I might have done that but I might not have done that. I don't know what was happening. I do not know this gentleman. If you showed him to me, I wouldn't know it was him. Please, I do not know my patients by their names. In 1991 we were a health centre and we did not do any complicated operations, because we did not have anaesthesia. We only did work in local anaesthesia. So I cannot give an answer whether I did or did not do this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the documents that I don't have copies in English, but I would like to ask the usher's assistance, if he would, to show the doctor that document. First I'd like to ask him some preliminary questions. This document has not been marked. This document has been in the possession of the Prosecution since 1996, as all of these documents have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When did it get -- when did this document get into your own possession?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: These documents were provided to the Prosecution by Mr. Brackovic in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So you must have had it since 1996 or so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have had them since 1996. I was counting on being able to make copies of these at the last minute, which I have not been able to. I really apologise to the Court, but the machine was broken all weekend and I had limited access yesterday. So I will provide copies in English. First I'd just like for him to authenticate it, then if he does authenticate it, then I will put this copy on the ELMO, so that everybody can see it and provide copies for the Chamber at our next break. Or, if the Court would so like, I would ask the Court if we could have a break now, just a 30 minute break, and I can have all the copies of every document provided for the Court and my cross-examination, I promise, will not take longer than 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You knew you were coming to Court this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did know I was coming to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From 9.00 until the time you came in you did not see fit to make copies of these? But that's not the argument. It should have been done before. Now, you have been in custody of this since 1996, no translations, no copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, do I have translations. I just don't have the copies made of it, Your Honour, at this moment. I will have them in 30 minutes. I am just asking the Court's tolerance. I really was expecting for Mr. Moran's direct examination to last until the break and at that time I would not have encountered this problem. But I am asking the Court's tolerance just to allow me to proceed under the circumstances as they exist right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Show him the Serbo-Croatian copy which we would not even understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, can you tell me if you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: This is a document. It is the so-called referral, and it is not a medical finding, and this finding is usually written on the back side of this document. It is a referral to a surgeon. It doesn't say which one or where this surgeon is. To dress a wound on the 2nd, 3rd and 4th finger of the right hand. This is a referral of the -- of a doctor, but this is not a document. Please. And we will be waiting in vain if you take a look at this. There is no finding of a surgeon who might have dressed this wound. There is no finding of the surgeon here. And, therefore, I cannot say anything further about this. This is just a referral to a surgeon. Without a record, whether the dress was wounded or not, if this is the only document you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No Dr. Buturovic, this is not the only document I have. This document is signed by Dr. Husein Alic, and you do know Dr. Alic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. He is my colleague, he is a future surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And this document is dated on February 20th, 1991, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's a referral for Mr. Esad Landzo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Well, you can show it to the Trial Chamber. It probably says so. The name probably is written on the document, but what I am saying is that there is no finding of the surgeon who dressed the wound. If have you that finding, you should show it. You shouldn't be hiding it. You should show that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I will get to that document next. All this is -- when he comes into the hospital, if he needs further surgery, this doctor refers him to the orthopaedic surgeon, who is you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you recognise Dr. Alic's referral to the orthopaedic surgeon at that point, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one copy of the English translation of this. I would like to distribute it to the Court, or, if you prefer, I can put it on the ELMO. He has testified that this is the referral to the only orthopaedic surgeon, who is this doctor at that hospital, and I would like to introduce that into evidence at this point. Here is the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Show the interpreter the copy, which he has -- which is the referral document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the original and the English interpretation of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This document is not in his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, it's in Dr. Alic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does he recognise his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you recognise Dr. Alic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Well, really, I don't know what to say. I cannot claim whether this is the handwriting of Dr. Alic. Are you asking me now -- if you are asking me now whether a patient had a wound in 1991, I can't really answer that. I cannot also answer whether this is or is not the handwriting of Mr. Alic. I cannot answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The question is do you recognise the handwriting of this doctor?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: It's difficult, you know. It might be. It might be his, but I would not claim it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Alic was a surgeon that was studying under you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are not familiar with his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will pass this and go to the next document, Your Honour. Thank you. If I could have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Please, let me just add one more thing. At the request of Mr. Brackovic, as far as I remember, also the same thing as for Mr. Delalic, I gave a -- I confirmed this based on a document that I found, so I am not claiming that he did not have this wound. I gave -- I might have given this finding. So is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I would like to distribute the English version of this copy, please, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: This one? This one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was given based on the documentation, based on the review of my documentation that I mentioned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Dr. Buturovic, does it bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to move that this document be entered into evidence at this point, for defence of Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, Dr. Buturovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be objecting to the introduction of this document, in part because it is a document created in 1996 at the request of Defence Counsel for Mr. Landzo having tentative medical opinions. And since this witness is not being called as a medical expert, he is being called as a fact witness, I believe whatever medical opinion he may have given the defence of Mr. Landzo in 1996, as part of the preparation for the defence case, is entirely irrelevant. And we would -- she has explicitly stated on several times that this witness will just be a fact witness. Now, if she wants to get into a few facts, I would not object to that, but this document also has various opinions and speculations of this doctor. In fact, he even says their assumptions, but he can't really say those things. So, it is entirely improper for this document to be admitted, and we would strenuously object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, but is it based upon the record relating to the years '91, '92?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a little -- it's a little unclear. There are parts of it that indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you can cross-examine him. You can cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear her explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is also the case that with respect to certain conclusions, he states, "There are no medical findings or documentation about that." And to the extent he's being called as an expert witness, and he's going to give his opinion, then we are not prepared for cross-examination about those issues. And that's why previously I brought this issue up. And Ms. McMurrey says he was only going to be a fact witness and was not going to be asked for any medical findings or conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is he the doctor who treated the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is the doctor who performed the surgery on Esad Landzo in February of 1991, and on the English interpretation there, that's the only one can I read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a fact, that he treated him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question of disability may be one of opinion, which he wouldn't give.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is coming here as a fact witness, and his document here, prepared in '96, says a review of the case history, file number 70-91. So this is a summary of his file of the incisions and the surgery that he performed on Mr. Landzo in 1991. The only thing that might even be construed as an opinion would be the conclusion at the bottom. I am only asking him to testify about the actual procedures that he performed on Mr. Landzo, which continues to keep him a fact witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would not object under those circumstances. And I would just ask that Defence Counsel subsequently redact the portions that have to do with his conclusion. But with those caveats, I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He can give evidence of what he did to the accused person, and that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So may I ask the Court to introduce this document into evidence to prove -- as proof of the surgery that was performed on Mr. Landzo in 1991? Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, can you tell us what kind of surgery, based on your -- refreshing your memory, with your case history file, 70-91, can you tell us about the surgery you performed on Mr. Landzo on February 21st, 1991, and the injuries that he suffered at that point?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Please, I told you, I do not remember this operation. I might have done it, or somebody in Sarajevo, maybe it wasn't me at all. I do not know that. If I did, we gave our opinion based on the documentation, which you have enclosed here at the very end. This was a cut, as I said, a cut of the second, third and fourth hand. I am reading this from the documents and I can say as a surgeon this is the sutura (Phon) tendons and the operations here are not very secure. They are not done that often and that even in the best hospitals in the world I do not know what was the finding of this gentleman, because I haven't seen him after that. As I said, we can only guess, but I have not seen anything after the operation. Please, you cannot ask me -- ask for me to give opinions and answer questions about things that I have not seen. As an expert, I can only talk about things that I have seen. And, usually, a surgeon does not really talk about his own findings, but about findings of other people. Therefore, I can talk about findings of other surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, I can't ask you to voice an opinion on findings of other surgeons, because you are not an expert witness in this trial for that purpose. You are only here to testify, and I am asking you to please tell the Court about, you did discuss the type of injury he sustained, and that was his right hand where the second, third and fourth tendons were severed in his hand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. This copy isn't very clear on this point. Yes, it says the second, third and fourth and fifth finger. Whether it is the fifth finger, I am not clear, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you performed surgery --

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I cannot claim this for sure, because the copy is very bad. The copy is bad. Because it is very important whether it's three or four fingers, but the copy is extremely bad. This copy that I got. Do you have a better copy? Do you have the original of this document which you copied, so that I can see. Because I don't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, I do not have the original. All I have is the copy that was given to me by Defence Counsel for me.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Okay. Poor me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And also, can you describe the kind of surgery you performed? Did you attempt to reconnect those tendons?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He already stated that he doesn't even know that he did any surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to rely on the document presented and signed by Dr. Buturovic as the best evidence as to what kind of injury and what kind of surgery was performed on Mr. Landzo in 1991. And I am going to move forward on this, because I don't believe the doctor is going to assist us in any further way on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (No microphone)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to ask -- could I ask Mr. Landzo to stand up in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, do you recognise this boy at all?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: No, I don't. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Landzo, could you hold up the injury on your right hand and show Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes. It is obvious -- you can obviously see now the results of the injury. There is a contraction, so there is -- the little finger and the finger next to it are cramped, and that is a reflection of his injury. But I do not have to know the patient. Maybe -- I might have operated on him, but now I can claim now that I have seen him, I can see that he did have this injury. The injury happened for sure, and there is -- there are no problems about that. And it has also been treated, and the results are obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you were the only orthopaedic surgeon in the Konjic health centre in 1991, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to -- and that was Defence Exhibit? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last one was Defence Exhibit D41/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that was admitted into evidence? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that the conclusion part of it is not admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like the assistance of the usher again to present another document to Dr. Buturovic, and the one English interpretation to the Chamber, please. And for the Prosecution, this is the attempted suicide in 1994, signed by Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D42/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic -- I am sorry. You had seen Mr. Landzo on another occasion, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: This finding is of my colleague, Radolvic (Phon), who is a psychiatrist in the hospital. She treated the patient and I signed this finding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to ask, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: What do you mean, do I recognise it? Well, this is probably a document from our hospital. Probably, because I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you do recognise your signature at the bottom of this document, do you not?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And can you tell me what this document is?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: No, because I am not an expert witness in psychiatry. No, I cannot. I signed this as a director, and not -- the director of the hospital, and as a psychiatrist, you can see in the right -- in the left angle of the -- in the left corner the signature of the psychiatrist, my colleague, Ms. Radolvic. She's the one who did this and not me. I am not the expert witness for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But Dr. Buturovic, the first paragraph represents medical procedures that were performed on Dr. -- on Mr. Landzo, and the second paragraph represents the findings of the neuropsychiatrist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There is only one psychiatrist working in our hospital, and this psychiatrist described and concluded this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but your conclusions are also represented in the first paragraph. That's why your signature is on this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: I signed it because I was the director of the institution, and I sign all documents, not just the ones pertaining to Landzo, but all the documents. As you know, in the normal world, there is a director of a Court and this director also signs all the documents. And I do the same thing in my hospital, as a director, this is a document of the hospital. And I signed it as a director of that hospital. And this is -- it is a document of the hospital and not a document of Dr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And as a director of the hospital, you read each document before you sign it, don't you, because this represents the medical procedures that you are representing occurred at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His position is very clear. He doesn't know personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His position is very clear. He does not know personally. This is a certificate prepared by the psychiatrist, and he signed it in his official capacity as a director, and not because he knew the facts personally, the facts given in the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first paragraph represents the medical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was prepared by the psychiatrist who must have prepared the history of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And whichever way you look at it -- he is here as a fact witness, and there is nothing he can say about this document other than his -- than is he a director of the hospital at the time this certificate was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, do you certify -- when you put your signature on a document, that that description of the medical procedures that took place actually happened? Isn't that why you put your signature on there as the manager and surgeon of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He says he has no personal knowledge he signed it, because the person concerned had signed it, and therefore he signed it as a director.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just asking, the first paragraph is not part of this neuropsychiatric report. It's what happened at the hospital, the physical procedures that occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This report was prepared by the psychiatrist, who also signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My conclusion about the report is that she prepared the second paragraph and he prepared the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The first paragraph, which represents the medical procedures that Mr. Landzo was put through when he appeared in 1994 in your hospital, that is why you signed this document, so you could say that those medical procedures occurred; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am the director of the hospital. I do not perform all duties and jobs in this hospital. We have over 200 employees at the hospital. We have five departments. What I do is I stand behind the overall work of the hospitals. I do not perform all examinations. There are departments who do that. I am director of the entire hospital, and I sign documents. This document came here and I signed it as a director, not as a person who performed this job -- work. I did nothing here. You keep insisting on something, and I do not know why you insist on this. You insist that I know Mr. Landzo. I wouldn't recognise him if I saw him in the street, if you can believe me. I performed no treatment on him. I am just -- I signed this as a director. I signed the document. I did not sign on, on a patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic, you wouldn't sign a document representative of your hospital if it contained lies, would you? It represents the truth, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sead Buturovic
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. No lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Buturovic's signature is affixed to this. I believe it's accurate and represents the occurrences of 1994. I would like to introduce this document into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Evidence of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As evidence of Mr. Landzo's mental state from the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His mental state. He does -- this does not even discuss his mental state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there can be presumptions drawn from the fact that he attempted to commit suicide in 1994 as a result of his arrest. And I believe it's very relevant to all of the scientific evidence that you are going to be hearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We've had so many of them. So many. Even since he's come here. We've had sufficient evidence of his mental state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, then, may I ask that this document be considered authenticated by Dr. Buturovic at this time, and you can reserve deciding whether it should be admitted into evidence because of relevance once you've heard the testimony in the Defence case. And it is marked D4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see what you're about. You're only saying at a certain time in -- I don't know what date it was then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's June 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There was certain procedures which we read he has attempted suicide. This is what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is exactly what I am trying to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then these documents should be admitted for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to have these documents admitted for the purpose of -- that certain procedures occurred and that certain things happened in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. This suggests that certain things happened and it was queried whether he was attempting suicide. That is all it says. It didn't say more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not sure, is the document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear the Prosecution's position in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's position is that this -- that this doctor can state that this is his signature. And we don't object to that. But with respect to the truth of the contents, we would object, because this doctor has stated that he has no information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All he has stated is as the doctor in charge of the hospital. He is obliged to sign all external documents, documents going out. And in this case the doctor who could be relied upon for the mental state, that is the neuropsychiatrist, has also signed. But if counsel is keen on proving the truth of this document, then he should know what next to do. Because Dr. Buturovic is not saying that the part signed by the neuropsychiatrist is true. He's not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I am not relying on the part of this document that reflects an opinion of the neuropsychiatrist. All I want reflected is the procedures that occurred, physical procedures that occurred to Mr. Landzo at the time that he was admitted to the hospital, and Dr. Buturovic said he would not sign any document that was not true. So I believe that the first paragraph -- I don't even mind redacting the part that refers to the neuropsychiatrist's opinion, but the first paragraph refers only to the factual procedures that occurred at that time and represents no opinion. And I am offering this document for that purpose only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the part you are offering for the mental state?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is the part that I am offering to show an occurrence that happened in 1994. The Court will have to draw their own opinion as to the mental state of Mr. Landzo, based upon the evidence that's put before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is your position. There is nothing wrong in that, if you are offering that as -- as certain things you have done to an accused person's, which is not stating any particular thing, could be regarded subsequently as exemplifying the mental state. If that is your position, I think one might admit it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Now, if the Court would just allow me to present one more document to Dr. Buturovic. And I am going to state that I am not quite sure whether the Prosecution has seen this document or not. It's -- would you, with your assistance, show that. It's a medical extract -- may I confer with the Prosecution just to see for a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I saw this document for the first time last night. I've been ranting and raving about the medical records of this person that I have not been able to find. But I did find an extract signed by Dr. Buturovic of this. I am not trying to ambush Ms. McHenry at all. So if the Court would like to take the break now, where they can have a chance to look at this document, I certainly would provide all of the copies to the Court, if we could return in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until 11.30. So we can have a break and return at noon. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I might, I believe the last document I was dealing with was D43; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, it was D43/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And could I have D43/4, the Bosnian version, given to Dr. Buturovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I am going to ask that any questions be in private session, because I believe that some of the things the Defence Counsel may get into refer to the private medical details of a witness. So I would just ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I told Ms. McHenry I have no objections to that. It's not a protected witness, but if it might offend somebody, I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Inform the technical crew to go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we'll go to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So let's have your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we call Nurko Tabak. Your Honour, while he is on his way in, remember, this is the second witness the Court ordered to appear today. He is the last witness we have for today. Dr. Bellas will appear tomorrow. And hopefully he will be done tomorrow afternoon. And then we will have our last witness, who is appearing by order of the Court on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, would you introduce yourself to the Court, tell them your name and where you are from.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Okay. My name is Nurko Tabak from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tabak, tell us a little bit about your background, for instance, are you a married man, and do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I am married and I am a father of two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And tell the Court a little bit about your education and background, just so they can get to know you.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I am a machine technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, during the summer and winter of 1992, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I worked in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what did you do in Celebici, sir?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I worked in a workshop for the upkeep of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And who was your superior while you were doing that?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Major Sefik Kevric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Major Sefik Kevric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But do you know what he did, what his position was? Was he the head of logistics for the TO, for instance, or was he something else --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may say, instead of Kevric, two or three times in the transcript it is written Karadzic, which is absolutely wrong, and therefore I would like to ask for the name to be entered correctly. Sefik, Kevric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you look behind you, you will see a model of the Celebici barracks and prison. Would you take a look at that and point out to us what building you worked in. You see it behind you? You can get up and just point to the building, if you'd like. And also, sir, before you take off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does he recognise this model? It's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask a specific question when he is standing there. It's easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, would you put on your earphones. Sir, do you recognise that as the Celebici, model of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand. Do I recognise what? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The model. That's a model of the Celebici barracks, right?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You recognise that? Okay. And the building you pointed to?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- that was the building that you worked in is right next door to hangar 6; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The building next to hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, I don't know if it was then, but today, or at least a year ago when I was there, there was -- both hangars are numbered hangar 6, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I am not sure if they are both called number 6. I know they were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, while you were working at the barracks repairing weapons, you did not come under the command of whoever was in command of the camp, did you? You worked directly for the major; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, I couldn't work for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Except for the major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, did you live on the barracks, or did you come every day and go to work and then go home?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I would come to work from home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And about what times did you generally work during the day?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: From 7, 7.30, until 4, 4.35, depending on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, again referring to the model. Could you show the judges how you got to the hangar where you worked. Well, first, let me back off. How did you get to the barracks? Did you drive your car?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I came by car, and I would come to the workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you drive your car all the way to the workshop?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, I would drive up to the workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you show the judges on the model the general route you took to get from the front gate to the workshop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He took the outer --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he took the outer drive. I just want to make sure the Court saw that thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember when prisoners first were detained in the Celebici barracks, roughly?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact date. I don't remember. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember whether it was -- in general terms, the first time you saw prisoners there, was it late May, early June, middle of June, middle of August, whatever you recall?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I think it was early June, as far as I remember, that it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were at the barracks, did you -- during the day, did you see the prisoners in hangar 6 being fed meals?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how many times a day did you -- did that happen in a normal occasion?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Twice, while I was there, breakfast and lunch. And I wasn't there for dinner, so, of course, I couldn't see dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you eat your breakfast and lunch at the barracks or either one, or both?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Both breakfast and lunch, or just lunch and just --

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: When I was there, both breakfast and lunch. When I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you see the prisoners eating their meals?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And tell the judges where they ate and what you saw in some detail about how they ate.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Well, I would see them eating in front of the hangar. There was a lawn, from the plates, just normally, from some small containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, sir, were they -- how many people did you see eating at one time, roughly?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen people, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, were they all eating out of the same pot, or did each one of them have his own plate?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly if they did -- those who did eat, yes, but I really don't know if they washed them more, what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But when the ten people were out there, were they all -- or 15 people, were they all eating out of the same pot or did each one have his own plate of food?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: They all had their plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And could you see the food from where you were?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Of course. I ate it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's the next question, was it the same kind of food that you were eating?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, was the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you have any estimate of the quantity of food that was provided to the inmates?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No. I think they got as much as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you see the -- well, was the food put onto the prisoners plates from a big pot? Did they have a big spoon or a ladle to put that food on?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, there was a ladle which was used to distribute the food with from a bigger container.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was the size of that ladle about the same size as the ladle that was used to dish food out to you?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same ladle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the food wasn't really tasty, was it? It was pretty bland food?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you see whether the prisoners had bread, sir?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I saw that they did have bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And could you get an idea of the size of the slices of bread that they had? Were they real thin slices, so thin you could almost see through them, or were they a substantial piece of bread?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I wasn't close to them. I did not have an opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough, sir. And, sir, the feeding that we just talked about, how the prisoners were fed, was that the same or pretty much the same the entire summer of 1992, or did it change from time to time?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I wouldn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you know my client, Mr. Delic, Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I know him a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I know him from the workshop in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You mean he was -- he would visit your workshop or you just saw him around? What do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I mean when he would come to us for a little bit of lubricant for the weapons and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, from the location where you were at -- strike that. Did you ever see any prisoners beaten, abused, burned up, stabbed, shot, hit with baseball bats, pickaxes, axe handles?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, not even the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any prisoners that looked like they had been beaten, burnt up, hit with axe handles, bruised all over?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anybody screaming like they were being beat up or burned up or --

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, because I did not have an opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you see the -- strike that. Sir, did you ever see any female prisoners in the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I did see them, but when I passed by the gate. But I wasn't sure whether they were prisoners or whether they had come for a visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned visits. Were the families of prisoners allowed to visit them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know how often those visits were?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Were they a fairly regular thing, or was it a rare event?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: A regular -- they were regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when they came to visit, did you see the families of the prisoners bringing packages of food or clothes or things like that to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you see or have occasion to see whether or not those packages were distributed to the prisoners or were they tossed into the river, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I don't think that they were thrown away. I think that they were given to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for instance, did you see the prisoners with clean clothes on, after a visit, or did you see them with food or smoking cigarettes or something like that after a visit?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I did see it once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: See what, sir? Clean clothes or smoking cigarettes or food or --

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Clean clothes and eating and smoking more than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, you say smoking more than usual. Was it a rare event to see one of the prisoners smoke a cigarette, or was it a fairly commonplace thing?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Well, at that time I could have seen it by accident. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but what I am getting at, was it common or uncommon to see one of the prisoners smoke a cigarette? Was it a very rare event, maybe you saw it once a month, or were they out on a fairly regular basis smoking cigarettes. I am not talking three packs a day, I am talking, were they available to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, they were available to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you know that because you saw them smoking them, right?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, what was the situation with water in the camp? Did you see -- was water freely available to everyone in the camp that you saw?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: As far as I could see, it was available to everyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What was the weather like in the summer of 1992? Was it hot or was it a mild summer or was it -- what was the weather like in general?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Hot. Hot. Hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you were working in one of those metal buildings, one of those metal hangars just like the prisoners were living in, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how hot was it inside there?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: I did not measure it. But it was hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Sir, do you know a woman named Grozdana Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, you've been informed, haven't you, that she accused you of sexually assaulting her?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Yes. And it is a great insult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, were there ever any of the women in the camp in your workshop while you were there?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, when you say it's a great insult that you've been accused of this crime, are you -- you are saying that you did not do it; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are having a -- it is your position, then, that you did not sexually assault Ms. Cecez, right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No, I did not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Sir, just because of the construction of the way sentences are sometimes in English we do funny things with how we put our sentences together, and they can, unless we are careful, they can have a backwards meaning. That's why I asked the question a second time. Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence of Mr. Delalic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence for Mr. Mucic has no questions for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Judge Jan, you see, it's not very much. I saw you looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because you didn't stand in your seat to ask the questions. I thought you had dozens of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Oh, I could do that, I really could. I'm sorry. Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Tabak, good day. I am Cynthia McMurrey, and I represent Esad Landzo. And you and I have never had an opportunity to meet or speak with one another before, have we?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have a few questions to ask you. It's my understanding that you and Mr. Landzo's mother came from the same village of Glavicine, I'm sure I mispronounced that, but are you from the same village as Mr. Landzo's mother?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: No. I am from Lucine, she is from Resitu (Phon).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In around the time of 1973, did your family and the Landzo family both live in a suburb of Konjic called Glavicine, next to each other, you were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Glavicine yes, Glavicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me?

utterances.speaker: Nurko Tabak
utterances.text: Glavicine. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
